ubo_and_aml_profiling.pep_and_sanctions_screening_protocols: Mandatory screening of all shareholders, directors, officers, and UBOs against the Canadian Consolidated Autonomous Sanctions List, United Nations Security Council sanctions, OFAC/OFSI-equivalent foreign sanctions, and Canadian PEP lists under PCMLTFA and FINTRAC guidance. Enhanced due diligence is required for politically exposed persons, family members, and close associates. OFAC/UN/Canadian sanction screening must be completed prior to incorporation and monitored on an ongoing basis.

statutory_name_clearance_protocol.registry_portal_name: Alberta Corporate Registry / Service Alberta (Corporate Registry System)
statutory_name_clearance_protocol.language_and_transliteration_doctrine: Proposed names must use the English/French/Roman alphabet or be a numbered name. Non-Latin script brand elements must be transliterated or translated into Roman characters. The name must be distinctive and not confusingly similar to existing registered names in Alberta. A NUANS name search report is required for incorporation.
statutory_name_clearance_protocol.extension_and_rejection_appeal_sop: If the proposed name is refused by the Alberta Corporate Registry, the applicant may file a Request for Reconsideration with the Registrar through Service Alberta within 30 days of the notice of refusal, attaching a revised NUANS report and written arguments showing distinctiveness and non-confusion. If the refusal is upheld, the applicant may apply to the Court of King's Bench of Alberta for judicial review. Alternatively, the applicant may file a fresh name request with a new NUANS report.

registered_office_and_commercial_substan.virtual_office_permissibility: For the corporate registered office, virtual office services are not sufficient. A physical street address in Alberta is mandatory for service of legal process and statutory notices. For a craft beer distribution business, a physical warehouse or licensed premises is also required to satisfy Alberta Gaming, Liquor and Cannabis Commission (AGLC) licensing and cold-chain logistics requirements.
registered_office_and_commercial_substan.physical_inspection_likelihood: Unannounced on-site inspections are moderately likely: 15%-25% annual probability for AGLC-regulated liquor premises. Routine registered office physical inspections are rare, under 5%, absent complaints or regulatory triggers.

incorporation_legal_framework.governing_statute_and_sections: Business Corporations Act (Alberta), RSA 2000, c B-9 (ABCA), ss. 10-13 (incorporation and articles), s. 101 (registered office), ss. 103-121 (directors and officers), ss. 148-165 (share capital; no minimum); alternative federal route under the Canada Business Corporations Act, RSC 1985, c C-44; liquor licensing under the Gaming, Liquor and Cannabis Act, SA 2008, c G-1.4, ss. 18-25; federal excise duty under the Excise Act, 2001, SC 2002, c 22
incorporation_legal_framework.competent_registry_authority: Registrar of Corporations, Alberta Corporate Registry, Service Alberta; online filing portal at corporate-registry.alberta.ca or via an Alberta-authorized service provider
incorporation_legal_framework.statutory_filing_instrument: Articles of Incorporation (Form 1) accompanied by Notice of Registered Office and Address for Service (Form 2) and Notice of Directors (Form 3)
incorporation_legal_framework.minimum_paid_up_capital_rule: No statutory minimum paid-up capital under the ABCA; shares may be issued for total consideration of not less than C$1.00. The Alberta registry does not require escrow of incorporation funds. However, the AGLC licensing review and commercial banking partners (Swift Wire and USD trade-payment rails) may require the corporation to evidence committed working capital of at least C$25,000 held in its Canadian operating account to support trade credit, inventory purchases and duty exposure.

national_tax_registration_infrastructure.competent_tax_authority: Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) / Agence du revenu du Canada (ARC); federal corporate income tax and GST/HST administered via CRA My Business Account portal (www.canada.ca/en/revenue-agency/services/e-services/e-services-businesses/business-account.html); Alberta Corporate Income Tax (ACT) is collected by the CRA for Alberta Treasury Board and Finance under the Tax Collection Agreement (Alberta Corporate Tax Act); liquor and excise licensing for beer distribution is split between the federal Excise Act, 2001 regime (CRA Excise Duty) and the Alberta Gaming, Liquor and Cannabis Commission (AGLC) for intra-Alberta sales.
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.tax_id_procurement_sop: A Canadian resident Business Corporation already holds a 9-digit CRA Business Number (BN) obtained at incorporation (via Corporations Canada or the Alberta Corporate Registry). For the craft beer wholesale/export mandate, the corporation must: (1) activate a GST/HST program account (RP suffix) through CRA My Business Account or Form RC1 once taxable worldwide supplies exceed CAD 30,000 in the preceding four consecutive calendar quarters, or voluntarily earlier; (2) activate a corporate income tax program account (RC suffix) to file T2 returns; (3) register with AGLC for a Manufacturer's Licence and, if selling to Alberta retailers, comply with AGLC mark-up and distribution rules (Alberta's privatized liquor model permits direct wholesale supply to licensed retailers); (4) obtain a federal excise licence and excise warehouse licence under the Excise Act, 2001 for beer removal, including zero- rated export removals; (5) if depositing funds from non-resident buyers, keep the FFI/IRP tax account in order for T106/T1134 filings where applicable. Non-resident shareholders do not require a Canadian TIN to hold shares, but non-resident corporate lenders/suppliers invoicing the Canadian entity require a CRA BN to avoid Part XIII gross-up issues.
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.default_entity_tax_classification: Entity_Level_Taxation; Territorial_Scope: a Canadian-resident corporation under common law residency or the deeming rule in ITA s. 250(4)(c) is subject to Part I federal tax on worldwide income (base federal rate 15%; reduced to 9% on the first CAD 500,000 of active business income for a Canadian-controlled private corporation) plus Alberta provincial corporate tax (general rate 8%; 2% on the small business limit of CAD 500,000 for qualifying CCPCs). Non-resident corporations with a Canadian permanent establishment are subject to Part I tax on Canadian-source business income and Part XIV branch tax (25%, reducible by treaty). The corporation is not a pass-through entity and is not eligible for US-style check-the-box; entity classification follows the statute and corporate law, with no elective transparency.
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.statutory_election_mechanisms: Canada does not provide check-the-box election; classification is statutory. Available mechanical elections include: ITA s. 85 rollover election on transfer of property to the corporation on a tax-deferred basis; ITA s. 88(2) winding-up election to crystallize subsidiary assets; ITA s. 256(9) associated-corporation designations affecting the CAD 500,000 SBD limit; ITA s. 216 election for non-residents on rental income; ITA s. 219 election for a non-resident corporation to be taxed under Part I instead of Part XIV branch tax; GST/HST elections include ETA s. 156 (associated persons deemed single supply), ETA s. 21 (closely related corporations election), and ETA s. 22 (zero-rated export election for non-resident registrants). Hybrid mismatch rules (ITA s. 18.4 and 18.6) apply to disallow deduction/non-inclusion outcomes; no elective de-hybridization regime exists, and denied amounts are not reversible by taxpayer election.

indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.indirect_tax_system_name: GST (Goods and Services Tax) – federal value-added tax under Part IX of the Excise Tax Act; Alberta has no provincial sales tax and no HST, so only the 5% federal GST applies on taxable supplies made in the province. Craft beer kegs sold for domestic wholesale are taxable at 5%; exports of beer are zero-rated under Schedule VI.
indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.statutory_registration_threshold_local_c: CAD 30,000 (small supplier exemption) measured on total worldwide taxable supplies, including those of associated persons, over the preceding four consecutive calendar quarters; threshold applies to both resident suppliers and non-resident suppliers of digital services or tangible personal property under the 2021 e-commerce measures; a person whose only supplies are zero-rated exports may apply to be a 'zero-rated exporter' and remain unregistered; proposed increase to CAD 50,000 has been announced but is not yet in force as of the current statute.
indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.electronic_invoicing_and_clearance_manda: No federal real-time fiscal clearance, digital stamping, or API-based e-invoice authorization mandate exists in Canada. CRA accepts paper, PDF, EDI, and PEPPOL-compliant e-invoices; the Pan-Canadian Trust Framework operates voluntarily on the PEPPOL network. Quebec has enacted a B2B mandatory XML e-invoicing regime (Revenu Québec) phased from 2026-2027 for large enterprises, but it does not apply to Alberta-based beer distributors absent Quebec sales. GST/HST returns are filed electronically through CRA GST Access or NETFILE; excise duty returns for beer are filed via the CRA Excise Duty Return portal. Exporters must file electronic export declarations through the Canadian Export Reporting System (CERS) within 15 days after the goods are exported to the CBSA.

export_zero_rating_and_refund_substantia.zero_rating_eligibility: Zero-rating applies to a supply of tangible personal property (craft beer kegs) made by the exporter where the supplier ships or delivers the goods to a place outside Canada, or makes the goods available to a common carrier for export under ETA Schedule VI, Part I, s. 5; the purchaser must be a non-resident and the property must leave Canada in the ordinary course of trade as a bona fide export. For services incidental to the beer export (e.g., cold-chain logistics, marketing fees), zero-rating applies if the service is supplied to a non-resident and is performed either entirely outside Canada or is not received in Canada under the place-of-supply rules. The exporter must obtain 'satisfactory evidence of export' at or before the time the goods are shipped and retain it for six years, per CRA GST/HST Memorandum 17.6.2, including bills of lading and customs export documentation; failure to hold contemporaneous documentary proof will cause the CRA to reassess the supply at 5% GST.
mandatory_customs_documentation_bundle: CBSA B13A Export Declaration or electronic export report filed via the Canadian Export Reporting System (CERS) showing commodity code 2203.00 for beer and the foreign country of destination
Commercial invoice issued by the Canadian exporter to the non-resident buyer showing the keg quantity, FOB/Ex-Works value in CAD, and zero-rated designation
Through Bill of Lading or Air Waybill naming a foreign discharge port or airport and evidencing physical departure of the consignment from Canada
Carrier or freight-forwarder certificate of export with the carrier's signature, date of departure, and vessel/flight number
Destination-country customs entry or import clearance document confirming the beer was cleared outside Canada
Inward Remittance Certificate, bank SWIFT MT103, or bank statement showing receipt of foreign currency proceeds from the non-resident buyer in the exporter's CAD account
export_zero_rating_and_refund_substantia.audit_scrutiny_and_clawback_penalties: Canada imposes no statute-codified FX repatriation deadline; 180 days is the operational benchmark under which the CRA expects to observe return consideration for export substantiation, but the absence of any receipt for a longer period will trigger audit scrutiny. CRA may deny zero-rating and assess 5% GST on the full export consideration, plus arrears interest (prescribed quarterly rate) and a civil penalty of 25% of the net tax under ETA s. 285; false or fraudulent statements attract a gross-negligence penalty under ETA s. 280.1 and, on conviction, fines up to 200% of the tax evaded or imprisonment up to five years (ETA s. 327.1). Income tax understatements from fictitious export revenue carry a 50% gross-negligence penalty under ITA s. 163(2). CRA audit of export zero-rating focuses on evidence contemporaneity, the exporter's status (licensed excise warehouse), and actual movement of kegs; beer exported without proper excise removal under the Excise Act, 2001 triggers excise duty assessment and potential seizure by the CBSA. Exporters failing to file the B13A within 15 days are subject to CBSA penalties under the Customs Act and the Export Reporting Regulations.

fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.central_bank_authority: Bank of Canada (Banque du Canada). Canada maintains no dedicated foreign-exchange control agency; exchange-control-related supervision is distributed among FINTRAC (anti-money-laundering and cross-border transaction reporting), OSFI (prudential regulation of deposit-taking institutions), Statistics Canada (balance-of-payments direct-investment reporting), and Global Affairs Canada (trade controls under the Export and Import Permits Act).
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.currency_convertibility_assessment: Canada provides full current-account and capital-account convertibility. There are no foreign-exchange controls, prior-approval mechanisms, profit-remittance barriers, or obligatory conversion requirements imposed on a federally incorporated Alberta business corporation exporting craft beer. Domestic and cross-border payments settle freely in CAD. Dividends paid to non-resident shareholders are subject to Part XIII withholding tax (25% statutory rate, potentially reduced to 5-15% under an applicable income tax treaty); managerial or service fees must withstand CRA re-characterization risks but are not blocked by exchange-control law.
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.export_proceeds_surrender_rules: Canada imposes no mandatory surrender of export proceeds, no statutory conversion ratio, and no deadline for repatriation or conversion of export receipts. Exporters must file electronic export declarations with the Canadian International Trade Single Window (CBSA) where applicable, file FINTRAC large-transaction/EFT reports for each cross-border wire of CAD 10,000 or more, and retain underlying shipping and invoice records for GST/HST and customs compliance. No central-bank approval is required to receive, hold, or convert USD export proceeds.

tier1_domestic_commercial_banks.account_class: Operating CAD Account (ACSS/Lynx clearing) plus USD Correspondent Account
Operating CAD Account and USD BusinessEdge Account; capital escrow sub-ledger
Operating CAD Account; USD cross-border treasury package; capital contribution escrow account
Operating CAD Account and USD Global Business Account; trade-services documentary collections
Operating CAD Account; USD convenience clearing; working-capital operating line readiness
Alberta-based Operating CAD Account and Capital Escrow Account with provincial affinity program

corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.fintech_emi_cross_border_viability: Medium-to-Low. Canada does not recognize the European-style EMI (Electronic Money Institution) as a distinct banking licence. A non-resident digital payment provider may lawfully serve the Alberta craft-beer distributor only if it: (i) registers with FINTRAC as a Money Services Business for each Canadian service location; (ii) complies with the Retail Payment Activities Act (RPAA) registration and risk-management rules once fully in force; and (iii) refrains from deposit-taking in the manner of a bank. Offshore EMIs cannot clear CAD directly into Payments Canada ACSS/Lynx rails without a Schedule I bank sponsor or a FINTRAC-registered pure-play MSB partner; accordingly, fintech rails are suitable for supplementary FX conversion and disbursements but not as the primary treasury backbone.
corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.physical_presence_and_kyc_interview_mand: No Canadian statute or federal regulation absolutely requires directors to appear physically in a branch. All major Schedule I banks permit remote opening for Alberta business corporations using certified corporate documents, notarized director identification, a board resolution authorizing signatories, and proof of an Alberta physical operating address. In practice, banks commonly require at least one director or authorized signatory to complete a live video identity interview and will apply enhanced due diligence where any 25%-plus beneficial owner or managing director is a non-resident. Documentary-only remote onboarding is achievable but generally limited to simpler single-purpose corporations with pre-existing Canadian banking relationships.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Non-resident beneficial ownership exceeding 25% with no demonstrated Canadian commercial nexus for a craft-beverage import/export business.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Certified passports and proof of residential address for every individual holding 25% or more; notarized ownership chain to ultimate natural persons; Alberta Corporate Registry search confirming active incorporation; AGLC (Alberta Gaming, Liquor and Cannabis) licence evidencing authority to distribute alcoholic beverages; audited or compiled financial statements; warehouse lease and Alberta operating address; corporate insurance certificates; detailed business plan with Canadian revenue projections.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Large inbound capital injection routed as a single high-value SWIFT wire within the first 60 days of account opening.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Subscription agreement, shareholder resolution, and updated share register evidencing the equity capital contribution; source-of-funds letter and bank statements of the remitting shareholder; MT103 wire message with matching beneficiary registry data; pro-forma supplier contracts and brewery offtake agreements demonstrating commercial deployment; CRA tax filings (initial corporate income tax return and notice of assessment); projected 24-month cash-flow statement.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Operating pattern inconsistent with microbrewery wholesale norms, such as rapid cash conversion, frequent cash deposits, or unannounced third-party payouts.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Aged accounts receivable and payable ledgers from licensed accounting software (QuickBooks or Xero Canada); serialized inventory and keg-tracking report reconciling brewing inputs to bottles/cans dispatched; landed-cost and freight documentation for cross-border keg supplies; monthly GST/HST returns and CRA excise duty account statements for beer volume; scheduled bank statements showing predictable, invoice-backed receipts.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Sanctioned jurisdiction or PEP-linked counterparty appearing in the distribution or logistics chain.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Complete list of material counterparties with legal identifiers and registration numbers; screen results against OSFI, FINTRAC, Global Affairs Canada, and OFAC consolidated sanctions lists; legal-counsel certification that each transaction is at arm's length and at fair market value; completed FINTRAC Politically Exposed Persons questionnaire executed by all directors; strengthened beneficial-ownership attestation confirming the absence of PEP equity.

cross_border_liquidity_and_clearing_rail.inbound_capital_injection_routing: Inbound equity capital must be routed by SWIFT MT103 to the Alberta operating account using the Canadian clearing structure: 3-digit institution number, 5-digit transit number, and 12-digit account number, together with the beneficiary bank's SWIFT/BIC. The payment narrative must state the purpose as 'Common Share Subscription — Equity Contribution to Canadian Business Corporation', and the remitting bank must complete FINTRAC EFT reporting where the transaction equals or exceeds CAD 10,000. Treasury must verify the funds against the AML/KYC acceptance dossier, record the share issuance in the corporate registry and minute book, and file any required Statistics Canada direct-investment reporting. Domestic further credits settle in T+1 via ACSS or same-day via Lynx; USD side letters can be cleared into a USD correspondent account.
cross_border_liquidity_and_clearing_rail.outbound_trade_disbursements: Export trade settlements should use: (i) SWIFT MT103 wires for high-value keg shipments, preferably with SWIFT gpi tracking; (ii) commercial letters of credit (MT700 issued or confirmed by a Schedule I bank) for large-border wholesale contracts; (iii) documentary collections (MT400/MT910) for contract-backed shipments where LC cover is not justified; (iv) USD clearing via U.S. Fedwire/CHIPS from Canadian-domiciled USD accounts; and (v) domestic direct debits through Payments Canada ACSS for routine Alberta hospitality and retail distributor collections. All outbound wire instructions must embed invoice references and be matched to underlying bills of lading and customs entries.
permissible_fx_hedging_instruments: Deliverable CAD/USD foreign-exchange forward contracts (1-12 month tenors) with a Schedule I bank under an ISDA 1998 Master Agreement
Cross-currency basis swaps (CAD/USD floating-floating) aligned with long-dated brewery expansion debt and capital-injection timelines
FX option collars (zero-premium tunnel structures) protecting conversion of USD export receivables into CAD
FX swaps (deliverable rollovers) for managing settlement-date mismatches between USD receivables and CAD operating disbursements
Non-deliverable forwards (NDFs) only where the counterparty currency is a restricted-convertibility currency outside the G10; CAD/USD and CAD/EUR must be hedged on a deliverable basis

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: Annual Return (Alberta Business Corporations Act, s. 117)
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Within 60 calendar days after the anniversary date of incorporation or registration
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Late filing fee approx. USD 74 (CAD 100); immediate administrative strike-off risk only after two consecutive unfiled years; loss of corporate existence prevents lawful distribution contracts.

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: T2 Corporation Income Tax Return (federal and Alberta corporate tax schedules attached)
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Within 6 months after fiscal year-end; e.g., December 31 year-end due June 30
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Late-filing penalty of 5% of unpaid balance plus 1% per month for up to 12 months; refund set-off withheld; gross negligence penalties 10%-50% of unpaid tax.

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: AGLC Liquor License Annual Renewal (brewery / manufacturer and wholesale distribution class)
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.receiving_authority: Alberta Gaming, Liquor and Cannabis Commission (AGLC)
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Annually on the license anniversary; renewal application and remittance due at least 30 days before license expiry
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Expiry of license upon non-renewal; immediate cessation of all wholesale beer distribution and export activity; late renewal treated as a fresh application with full public consultation and processing delays.

statutory_audit_and_accounting_mandate.compulsory_audit_thresholds: Non-distributing private corporations may waive the mandatory audit by unanimous shareholder consent under ABCA if no securities have been distributed to the public; distributing corporations and all public-reporting entities must appoint an independent auditor. CRA may also request audited financial statements in high-risk situations.
statutory_audit_and_accounting_mandate.governing_accounting_framework: Canadian GAAP – Accounting Standards for Private Enterprises (ASPE) for private corporations; IFRS mandatory for publicly accountable enterprises or federally distributing corporations.

corporate_registers_and_ubo_annual_confi.ubo_annual_confirmation_protocol: Alberta's ABCA requires a Register of Individuals with Significant Control (ISC). There is no annual government filing of this register, but the board must, at least once per year and upon any share transfer, update and confirm the ISC information; the signed confirmation is preserved in the Minute Book.
mandatory_on_site_statutory_registers: Register of Individuals with Significant Control (ISC)
Register of Officers and By-Law Entries

recurring_annual_maintenance_budget_usd.statutory_audit_estimated_fee_usd: USD 2,500–7,500 for a small private corporation if audit is required or voluntarily engaged

corporate_income_tax_regime.statutory_headline_rate: 23% combined (15% federal general rate + 8% Alberta general rate); reduced to 11% combined (9% federal + 2% Alberta) on the first CAD 500,000 of qualifying active business income of a Canadian-controlled private corporation (CCPC) under the Small Business Deduction.
corporate_income_tax_regime.effective_tax_rate_incentives: CCPC Small Business Deduction (federal 9% and Alberta 2% on first CAD 500,000 active business income per associated group); federal SR&ED investment tax credits (ITCs) at 33% for qualifying expenditures of CCPCs; federal Clean Technology ITCs; Alberta Investor Tax Credit and Alberta Small Business Investment Tax Credit; accelerated capital cost allowance (e.g., Class 43.2 clean energy equipment); no Alberta provincial retail sales tax (end-user distribution logistics exempt from PST/HST at the corporate level except GST/HST collection duties); arm's length interest exemption from Part XIII withholding.

tax_return_filing_anatomy.form_identifier_and_portal: T2 Corporation Income Tax Return filed electronically via the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) EFILE portal through certified tax preparation software; Alberta provincial income tax is integrated into the T2 and the Alberta-specific schedules (T2 Schedule 3 and Schedule 125) under the federal-provincial tax collection agreement; T2 is due for the Alberta business corporation even if gross revenue is nil.
tax_return_filing_anatomy.statutory_deadline_rule: Filing deadline is no later than 6 months after the fiscal year-end (e.g., a December 31 year-end must file by June 30 of the following calendar year). Payment of the final balance of tax is due no later than 2 months after fiscal year-end for a non-CCPC and 3 months after fiscal year-end for a CCPC claiming the small business deduction; instalments are due quarterly for most CCPCs and monthly for larger corporations (taxable capital above CAD 10 million).

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Corporation legal name, 9-digit Business Number (BN) with program account RC0001, fiscal year-end, jurisdiction of incorporation (Alberta), mailing address, directors' names and addresses, and the principal business activity code (NAICS 424810 / ISIC 4632 for craft beer wholesale distribution).
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: A non-resident corporation carrying on business in Alberta through a permanent establishment (PE) must complete the identification area, indicate the Alberta PE address, and note that it is not a CCPC; a Canadian agent or officer having custody of records in Canada must sign.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.line_or_box_code: T2 Page 1 - Box 010 through Box 160 (Elections and Status)
field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Check-box elections for deemed residency, international agreements, and the CCPC status declaration; the corporation must certify whether it is a CCPC, whether the 500,000 small business limit is available, and whether it has any cross-border transactions requiring Schedules 21 or T106.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: A non-resident corporation with a PE in Alberta is not a CCPC and must mark the relevant box; any transaction with a non-arm's length non-resident is reportable on a separate T106 return regardless of the entity's resident or non-resident status.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Computation of net income for income tax purposes: gross wholesale revenue from hazy IPA keg distribution, minus cost of goods sold (hop raw materials, brewing inputs, kegs, cold-chain freight), operating expenses (warehouse leases, trucking, tariffs), amortization, and other deductions; adjust GAAP financial statement income for tax-specific items such as meals, entertainment, and capital gains.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: The non-resident taxpayer must compute net income attributable to the Alberta PE only; use Form T2225 and allocate business income using the PE formula; expenses headquarters charged to the branch must satisfy arm's length reasonableness and Canadian source attribution.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Taxable income after applying deductions, including the non-capital loss carryover (Schedule 11), capital loss deductions limited to allowable capital losses, and the prior year losses; enter the taxable income amount that will be carried to the federal and provincial tax computations.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Non-resident corporations may claim non-capital losses incurred in Canada against Canadian-source taxable income and allocate them to provinces; the foreign tax credit (Schedule 21) applies only for foreign income included in Canadian taxable income.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.line_or_box_code: Line 360 to Line 428 - Federal Part I Tax Calculation
field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Federal Part I tax: taxable income at 38%, less the 10% provincial abatement, less the 13% general rate reduction for non-CCPCs, and less the 19% small business deduction for CCPC eligible income; yields the effective 15% federal general rate or 9% federal small business rate; add refundable Part I.3 and special taxes where applicable.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: A non-resident corporation not resident in a province (no PE) pays the 38% federal rate reduced only by the general rate reduction, without the 10% provincial abatement, unless it demonstrates that the income is subject to tax in Alberta.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Detailed federal computation: taxable income in column A; federal tax at 38%; deduct the 10% provincial abatement (column B), the general rate reduction (column C), and the small business deduction (column D); then subtract investment tax credits, including SR&ED ITCs from Schedule 31.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Non-resident corporations complete Schedule 1 only to the extent of Canadian-source business income through a PE; the provincial abatement is capped at 10% of income allocated to a province, and a PE allocation schedule must be attached.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Alberta provincial tax: taxable income allocated to Alberta at 8% general rate; for a CCPC, 2% applies to the first CAD 500,000 of active business income allocated to Alberta, with the business limit prorated across associated corporations and across provinces using the PE formula.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: A non-resident with an Alberta PE must allocate taxable income to Alberta using the PE formula and complete Schedule 3; the Alberta small business deduction is unavailable to non-residents because the entity is not a CCPC.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.line_or_box_code: Schedule 11 and Schedule 4 - Loss Reconciliation and Business Limit
field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Schedule 11 reconciles current-year non-capital losses, restricted farm losses, and net capital losses carried over and applied to reduce taxable income; Schedule 4 determines the CCPC business limit for the small business deduction, including the associated-company aggregation and the CAD 15 million taxable capital phase-out.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: A non-resident entity cannot claim the CCPC business limit; losses incurred in Alberta are eligible for the 20-year non-capital loss carryforward, but the loss claim must be filed within the 3-year carryback or 20-year carryforward windows.

tax_return_filing_anatomy.failure_penalties: Late filing of the T2 incurs a penalty of 5% of the unpaid balance plus 1% per full month of delay, capped at 12 months (total up to 17%); if the CRA issues a demand to file, the penalty is doubled (10% plus 2% per month, up to 29%). For a year with no balance owing, the penalty is CAD 100 per day up to CAD 2,500. Unpaid tax is subject to compound daily prescribed interest (currently approximately 8% annually). Failure to file an information return such as T106 triggers CAD 100 per day per form (maximum CAD 2,500 per form). The transfer pricing penalty under s. 247(3) of the Income Tax Act is 10% of the net adjustment amount when the adjustment exceeds the greater of CAD 250,000 or 10% of gross revenue, in addition to the reassessed tax and interest.

profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.statutory_dividend_wht_rate: 25% Part XIII withholding tax on the gross amount of dividends, deemed dividends, and surplus distributions paid to a non-resident shareholder from Canadian sources. Under the Canada-US Tax Treaty, the rate is reduced to 5% for a US resident beneficial owner that is a company holding at least 10% of the voting stock of the Canadian payer, and to 15% in all other cases; Alberta does not impose a separate provincial dividend withholding tax, so the Part XIII federal rate is the sole statutory rate.
profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.treaty_relief_application_protocol: To invoke treaty relief, the non-resident recipient must complete CRA Form NR301 (Declaration of Eligibility for Benefits Under a Tax Treaty for a Non-Resident Taxpayer) and provide an original or certified copy of the Tax Residency Certificate (TRC) issued by the treaty-country tax authority. The Canadian payer must obtain and retain the NR301 and TRC before making the payment, reasonably assess the beneficial ownership and limitation-on-benefits provisions, withhold at the reduced treaty rate if valid, and report the payment on Form NR4 and the NR4 Summary filed with the CRA. If the payer failed to withhold correctly, the non-resident may file Form NR7 to request a refund or reduction, but the Canadian payer remains jointly and severally liable for the unremitted Part XIII amount, interest, and penalties under s. 215 of the Income Tax Act.
profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.cross_border_royalty_and_interest_wht: Statutory Part XIII withholding is 25% for royalties paid to non-residents for the use of intangible property (including beer brand trademarks, brewing processes, and proprietary hazy IPA recipes) and 25% for interest paid to non-arm's length non-residents. Arm's length interest paid to a non-resident who deals at arm's length with the payer and does not share in the profits is generally exempt from Part XIII. Under the Canada-US Treaty, royalty rates are reduced to 10% (0% for copyright and patent royalties) and interest to 15% generally, with a 0% rate for Canadian government interest and certain related-party arm's length arrangements; treaty claims require the NR301 and TRC protocol described above.

transfer_pricing_and_economic_substance.tp_documentation_threshold_local_currenc: CAD 250,000: Form T106 (Transfer Pricing Return) must be filed for reportable transactions with each non-arm's length non-resident when the aggregate value of transactions within any category (goods, services, interest, royalties) exceeds CAD 250,000 in the fiscal year. Contemporaneous transfer pricing documentation (equivalent to the OECD Transfer Pricing Documentation Master File and Local File) must be prepared and retained by the taxpayer when this threshold is exceeded and an arm's length price is relied upon. Country-by-Country (CbC) reporting under Form T1173 is mandatory for MNE groups with consolidated group revenue of CAD 1 billion or more in the preceding fiscal year. The Alberta-based craft beer distributor should treat any sales of kegs, licensing of brewing trademarks, or intercompany distribution services with US affiliates as reportable transactions subject to the CAD 250,000 threshold.
transfer_pricing_and_economic_substance.economic_substance_doctrine: Canada and Alberta do not apply the UAE-style Economic Substance Regulations (ESR), but the Income Tax Act contains an equivalent anti-avoidance architecture: the General Anti-Avoidance Rule (GAAR, s. 245) nullifies tax benefits from 'avoidance transactions' lacking genuine economic substance, business purpose, and a bona fide non-tax purpose. The CRA applies a substance-over-form analysis to disregard shell corporations, treaty-shopping conduits, and circular financing arrangements. For a craft beer distribution entity, the CRA will examine whether the Alberta corporation has real employees, physical premises, actual inventory, cold-chain distribution activity, and arms'-length contracts; a 'zombie' entity with no operational substance and only intercompany paper invoices is vulnerable to GAAR reassessment, re-attribution of profits to the Canadian shareholder, and denial of treaty benefits.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: Tax Evasion (Income Tax Act s. 239 and Criminal Code s. 380)
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Willfully evading or attempting to evade federal or Alberta corporate income tax by filing a false or misleading T2 return, concealing Swift-wire sales revenue from overseas distribution, inflating cost of goods sold for craft beer inputs, fabricating supplier invoices, destroying books and records, or participating in a deliberate underground cash scheme.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: On indictment: a fine of 50% to 200% of the tax evaded plus imprisonment for up to 5 years; on summary conviction: a fine of up to CAD 50,000 plus imprisonment for up to 2 years. The CRA will also assess a 50% gross negligence penalty on the understated income and charge compound daily interest on all unpaid amounts from the due date until payment is made.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors who sign false returns or direct fraudulent conduct are personally exposed: the CRA lifts the corporate veil under s. 227.1 for unremitted source deductions and Part XIII amounts, and under s. 160 for transfers to non-arm's length parties. Directors may face civil restitution, garnishment of personal assets, travel bans via CBSA flagging on outstanding tax debts, and imprisonment for fraud over CAD 5,000 under Criminal Code s. 380.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: Failure to Withhold and Remit Part XIII Non-Resident Tax
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Paying dividends, deemed dividends, royalties, management fees, or non-arm's length interest to a US parent or non-resident beneficiary without withholding the 25% statutory rate or without validly documenting a treaty-reduced rate through Form NR301 and the Tax Residency Certificate.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: The Canadian payer is liable for the full unwithheld Part XIII amount plus arrears interest and a 10% penalty on the amount not withheld; daily penalties apply for failure to remit or report on Form NR4; the CRA may also assess the non-resident directly but will not discharge the payer's liability until recovery is exhausted.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors are jointly and severally liable under s. 227.1 for the unremitted Part XIII withholding if the corporation fails to pay; the CRA can issue a compliance hold on bank accounts, garnish receivables, and pursue the directors' personal bank accounts and real property without a court order when the 2-year limitation window has passed.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Entering into non-arm's length cross-border transactions (e.g., selling kegs to a related US distributor at below-market prices, paying excessive royalties for the hazy IPA brand, or charging non-arm's length management fees) without preparing contemporaneous documentation and without filing Form T106 when the CAD 250,000 threshold is exceeded.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: A penalty of 10% of the net transfer pricing adjustment is imposed when the adjustment exceeds the greater of CAD 250,000 or 10% of the taxpayer's gross revenue; the penalty is in addition to the reassessed tax, interest, and any 50% gross negligence penalty; the CRA can also impose penalties under s. 162 for failure to file T106 or for incomplete information.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors who sign a false or misleading T106 declaration or who knowingly set non-arm's length prices that strip profits out of Canada can be held personally liable where the corporation is insolvent; the CRA will look through the corporate shield when the company is a mere conduit and the directors have engaged in a sham pricing arrangement.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: AML / Proceeds of Crime (PCMLTFA and Criminal Code s. 462.31)
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: A craft beer wholesale distributor handling large Swift-wire and local direct debit payment rails does not qualify for a mandatory FINTRAC reporting entity designation unless it acts as a money services business, but it remains subject to the Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Act if it engages in suspicious transactions or accepts cash amounts of CAD 10,000 or more; failing to maintain a compliance program, assess money laundering risk, or report suspicious transactions to FINTRAC triggers liability.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Administrative Monetary Penalties (AMPs) of up to CAD 1 million for a corporation and up to CAD 200,000 for individuals, imposed per violation with no requirement of criminal intent; failure to report a large cash transaction or a suspicious wire transfer is a separate violation; criminal money laundering charges carry imprisonment of up to 10 years on indictment.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors and officers who knowingly fail to implement AML controls can be personally named in FINTRAC AMPs and prosecuted under Criminal Code s. 462.31; a conviction leads to criminal fines, imprisonment, forfeiture of corporate assets, and a travel ban enforced by the Canada Border Services Agency. Although the standard risk tier is low, the entity must document the risk assessment and annual training records.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: Shell Company / GAAR and Economic Substance Failure
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Operating an Alberta business corporation with no physical premises, no employees, no real inventory or cold-chain activity, and no bona fide commercial purpose, created solely to interpose an intermediary for tax deferral, treaty shopping, or avoidance of Canadian tax on distribution profits; paying excessive fees to a non-resident affiliate while booking continuous losses in Canada.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: The CRA applies GAAR (s. 245) to deny the tax benefit and reassess on a substance-over-form basis; a 15% GAAR penalty may be imposed on the denied tax benefit under the 2024 proposed amendments; the sham doctrine permits the courts to void the entire arrangement; the corporation's residence and PE status will be re-analyzed and all cross-border payments recharacterized as taxable Canadian-source income.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors who cause the corporation to be a 'zombie' shell are exposed to personal liability under s. 160 for the tax benefit transferred, s. 227.1 for any unremitted amounts, and the general law of fraudulent conveyance when the veil is pierced; the CRA may also obtain a travel ban under s. 226.1 and criminal prosecution for tax evasion where the shell was a deliberate artifice to conceal taxable income.
